questions.q: In a star topology with 15 nodes connected to a central switch, how many dedicated point-to-point links exist between nodes and the central device?
questions.a: 15 links. Each node has exactly one dedicated cable connecting it to the central switch. A common wrong answer is 105 (calculating 15×14/2), which reveals the student is confusing star topology with mesh topology where every node connects to every other node. Another error is 14, thinking the central device doesn't count as a connection endpoint. The correct reasoning: count the cables radiating from the switch — one per node.

questions.q: A student claims: "Star topology is better than bus topology because it uses less cable." Is this statement correct? Explain why or why not.
questions.a: The statement is incorrect. Star topology typically uses MORE cable than bus topology because each node requires a separate cable run to the central device, whereas bus topology uses a single backbone cable with short drop cables. A student who agrees reveals a misconception that "better" always means "less cable." The trade-off: star spends more on cabling to gain fault isolation, easier troubleshooting, and higher performance. The correct comparison: star = higher cabling cost, bus = lower cabling cost but single point of failure on the backbone.

questions.q: In a star network using a hub (not a switch), Node A sends a data frame to Node B. Describe the exact path the frame takes and what the hub does with it.
questions.a: Path: Node A → dedicated cable → Hub → broadcasts frame out ALL other ports → dedicated cables → all nodes (including B) receive it. Node B accepts it; others discard it after checking destination MAC. A wrong answer like "Hub sends it only to Node B" reveals confusion between hub (Layer 1 repeater, broadcasts) and switch (Layer 2, forwards selectively). Another error: "Frame goes A → Hub → B directly" misses the broadcast nature of hubs. Key insight: hubs create a single collision domain; switches create separate collision domains per port.

questions.q: Compare the fault tolerance of star topology vs bus topology when: (a) one node's network cable is cut, (b) the central device (hub/switch) fails, (c) the backbone cable in bus topology is cut. Present as a 3-row comparison table.
questions.a:
| Failure Scenario | Star Topology Impact | Bus Topology Impact |
|------------------|---------------------|---------------------|
| (a) One node cable cut | Only that node disconnected; rest unaffected | Only that node disconnected; rest unaffected |
| (b) Central device fails | ENTIRE NETWORK DOWN — single point of failure | N/A (no central device) |
| (c) Backbone cable cut | N/A (no backbone) | ENTIRE NETWORK DOWN — single point of failure |

A student who says "star has no single point of failure" misses the central device vulnerability. A student who says "bus is more fault-tolerant" ignores that both have single points of failure, just at different locations. The nuanced answer: star isolates node failures better but concentrates risk at the center; bus distributes risk along the backbone but any backbone break kills all.

questions.q: A small business has 8 workstations, 1 server, and 1 network printer. They currently use bus topology with coaxial cable. The owner wants to upgrade to star topology using Cat6 UTP and a 16-port switch. Evaluate this upgrade proposal on four criteria: (1) cabling cost, (2) future scalability, (3) fault isolation, (4) performance for file transfers to the server. Justify each.
questions.a: (1) Cabling cost: INCREASES — star requires 10 separate Cat6 runs (8 workstations + server + printer) vs one coaxial backbone with 10 short taps. Cat6 is pricier than coax per meter. (2) Scalability: IMPROVES — adding an 11th device means one new cable run to switch; bus requires tapping backbone (disrupts network) and signal degradation limits nodes. (3) Fault isolation: IMPROVES — cable cut affects one device; bus backbone cut kills all. (4) Performance: IMPROVES — switch provides dedicated 1 Gbps per port (full duplex); bus shares 10 Mbps half-duplex with collisions. Overall: upgrade justified despite higher initial cabling cost.

questions.q: Design a star topology network for a 3-floor office building with 12 workstations per floor. Each floor has a wiring closet. You have one central server room in the basement. Sketch the hierarchy (text description OK) and specify: (a) where switches go, (b) how floors connect to basement, (c) what cabling standard you'd use for horizontal vs backbone runs, (d) one reason to use a core switch in basement vs connecting all floor switches directly to server.
questions.a: (a) One 16-port access switch per floor in each wiring closet (12 workstations + 1 uplink + 3 spare). (b) Each floor switch uplinks via fiber (or Cat6a) to a core switch in basement server room. (c) Horizontal runs (switch to workstation): Cat6 UTP (100m max). Backbone runs (floor switch to core): Cat6a or multimode fiber (OM3/OM4) for 1/10 Gbps over longer distances. (d) Core switch aggregates traffic, provides single management point, enables VLANs/inter-VLAN routing, and reduces server port count — connecting 3 floor switches directly to server would need 3 server NICs/ports and no traffic aggregation. A flat design (all to server) lacks scalability and traffic control.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Star topology is a network ______ where all nodes (computers, printers, servers) are individually connected to a central connecting device (hub or switch) via dedicated point-to-point links, forming a star-like structure where the central device manages all data transmission between nodes.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you're setting up a ______ lab for 30 students in your school.
What is Star topology? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Star topology is a network configuration where all nodes (computers, printers, servers) are individually connected to a central connecting device (hub or switch) via dedicated point-to-point links, forming a star-like structure where the central device manages all data transmission between nodes.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagine you're setting up a computer lab for ______ students in your school.
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Star topology?
questions.a: Students often believe "star topology has no single point of failure" because they focus on node-level fault isolation (one cable cut doesn't affect others).

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to: (1) Draw and label a star topology diagram showing central hub/switch, nodes, and transmission media; (2) Explain how data flows from source to destination via the central device; (3) Compare star topology with bus topology on at least four parameters (fault tolerance, cabling cost, scalability, performance).
